title: Endorsements and Logbook Entries
summary: Connect every signature to the training, proficiency, privilege, and regulation it actually certifies.
objectives: Distinguish a training entry from an authorization to exercise a privilege.
Audit a student’s solo, cross-country, and practical-test eligibility.
Use the current AC 61-65 and the underlying regulation instead of memorizing sample numbers.
Track instructor records and recent experience without treating a lapse as permission to keep teaching.

sections.title: What a logbook entry proves
sections.body:
A logbook preserves evidence. Record the experience needed to support a certificate, rating, flight review, or recent-experience requirement. For the applicable entry, identify the date, duration, departure and arrival locations, aircraft identification, experience category, and operating conditions. Include the safety pilot when required.

For instruction, describe what was actually taught and record the training time. The authorized instructor signs the entry and identifies their certificate and applicable expiration or recent-experience end date. “Flight lesson, 1.0” tells the next instructor little about the student’s competence. “Crosswind approach, rejected landing, and go-around decision making” makes the training traceable.
sections.deep: Why: Time is an accounting category; proficiency is a demonstrated capability. An hour of training does not automatically authorize solo flight. Likewise, logging PIC and acting as PIC are different legal questions. Determine both from the applicable rule before entering a time category. An electronic logbook is useful only when its entries, signatures, and backups preserve the same evidence.

sections.title: The first-solo decision
sections.body:
Build a chain rather than collecting signatures: verify student eligibility and documents, complete the pre-solo knowledge test and review incorrect answers, provide and log the required training, and assess safe proficiency in the relevant make and model. Then issue the required solo authorization with limitations that fit the student and conditions.

The recurring student-solo authorization uses a 90-day window. A student who changes make and model needs the applicable training and authorizations for that aircraft. A student certificate or an old successful solo does not replace them. Citizenship or security-training requirements, medical eligibility when applicable, and school procedures are separate checks that belong in the instructor’s preparation.
sections.deep: Apply it: A student flies excellent landings in calm weather but has never managed a gusty crosswind. Their competence today does not justify an unrestricted wind limit. Document specific limits, verify that the student understands them, and explain what change requires another conversation. Limitations make the authorization reflect the training actually completed.

sections.title: Local solo and cross-country are different permissions
sections.body:
A basic solo authorization does not automatically permit a new destination or a longer route. Under §61.93, identify whether the proposed flight needs general cross-country proficiency, a flight-specific planning review, or qualifies for a defined nearby-airport or repeated-route provision. Those provisions have their own training and endorsement conditions.

For an ordinary student solo cross-country, the planning-review endorsement addresses that flight and the existing conditions. Review weather, route, performance, fuel, airspace, alternatives, and the student’s limitations. If the destination, route, or conditions change materially, reassess the plan rather than assuming yesterday’s signature covers today’s flight.
sections.deep: Why: General training establishes the student’s ability to plan. A flight-specific review checks the actual plan and environment. The two answer different questions. For example, training to land at an airport within 25 NM for takeoff-and-landing practice is a defined exception, not a blanket authorization to fly any 25-NM mission. Read the full provision before using it.

sections.title: Recommend the applicant, not a stack of hours
sections.body:
For a practical test, compare the applicant’s documents and logged experience with the applicable certificate, category, class, and training rules. Verify the knowledge-test requirement, recent preparatory training under §61.39, readiness, and review of knowledge-test deficiencies as applicable. The instructor’s recommendation certifies preparation, not just that minimum hours were accumulated.

Use the current AC 61-65K as a wording guide, then read the cited regulation. Sample endorsement numbers are navigation aids that can change between revisions. Do not apply a universal “60-day endorsement expiration”: solo authorizations, test prerequisites, flight reviews, and aircraft qualifications have different rules.
sections.deep: Apply it: For an added category or class, begin with §61.63 and the applicant’s existing privileges. Then identify required training, aeronautical experience, knowledge testing, practical testing, and any authorization needed while training. An additional class may have no specified minimum training time in that provision while still requiring demonstrated proficiency. Avoid the shortcut that all add-ons follow one endorsement package.

sections.title: Keep the instructor’s own audit trail
sections.body:
The student’s logbook and the instructor’s retained records serve different purposes. Under §61.189, the instructor retains the required solo-endorsement records and knowledge/practical-test endorsement records, including the prescribed dates and test results, for at least three years. Keep records retrievable even if the student leaves the school or loses a logbook.

A useful working record identifies the student, authorization, applicable aircraft, limitations, date, and supporting proficiency assessment. Check your own instructor privileges and limitations before signing. A current pilot certificate alone does not establish authority to give every kind of instruction or endorsement.
sections.deep: Why: A later reviewer should be able to reconstruct what you authorized and why. An endorsement copied from an old template can contain the wrong aircraft, rule, or instructor date even when the underlying training was sound. Audit the completed text, not just the template heading. School record systems support this process but do not remove the individual instructor’s responsibility.

sections.title: CFI recent experience and reinstatement
sections.body:
For certificates issued without an expiration date, the certificate and the authority to exercise its privileges are separate. §61.197 requires qualifying recent experience within the applicable 24-calendar-month period. Available pathways include specified practical tests, an approved FIRC, qualifying instructional activity, and other listed provisions. Check the complete pathway and required FAA documentation.

If recent experience lapses, stop exercising instructor privileges until properly reinstated. §61.199 allows an approved FIRC route when no more than three calendar months have passed since the recent-experience period ended. Beyond that, the ordinary reinstatement routes require the prescribed practical test. This is a reinstatement opportunity, not three extra months of instructor privileges.
sections.deep: Why: The early-completion window in §61.197 can preserve the existing month, while the post-lapse provision in §61.199 addresses lost privileges. Confusing those windows creates an illegal-instruction risk. Track the end month, the completion date, and FAA processing requirements explicitly. Older certificates printed with an expiration date also require attention to the transition provisions.

teachBack: Explain why a signed training entry is insufficient by itself for a first solo.
Audit a proposed solo cross-country and identify what each required authorization certifies.
Explain the difference between a CFI recent-experience period and certificate duration.
takeaways: Start with the proposed privilege and applicable rule, then document the training and proficiency.
Authorization periods vary; there is no universal endorsement expiration.
Keep the instructor’s required records for at least three years.
A lapse in instructor recent experience stops privileges until reinstatement.

quiz.question: A student’s logbook shows a signed hour of landing instruction. What does that entry establish by itself?
options: The described training was received.
The student may solo in any airplane.
The student has passed a practical test.
The student has unrestricted cross-country privileges.
feedback: A signed training entry documents the instruction and time recorded; separate authorizations govern privileges.
Solo permission requires the applicable proficiency and make/model endorsements.
A training entry is not a record of passing a practical test.
Cross-country privileges depend on additional training and the applicable authorizations.
quiz.hint: Separate evidence of instruction from permission to act.

quiz.question: A student’s most recent recurring solo authorization is 91 days old. All other documents are valid. What is required before another solo?
options: Only the student’s assurance that proficiency is unchanged.
A new applicable solo authorization following the required instructor determination.
A private-pilot knowledge test instead of another endorsement.
A flight review endorsement instead of a solo authorization.
feedback: The student cannot extend an authorization through self-assessment.
The recurring solo authorization must satisfy its 90-day requirement and proficiency conditions.
The private knowledge test does not renew student solo authorization.
A flight review is a different regulatory process.
quiz.hint: Check the authorization’s own time window.

quiz.question: A student has general solo cross-country training. An ordinary new solo cross-country is planned, with no repeated-route exception. What does the flight-specific endorsement add?
options: A permanent exemption from weather review.
Permission to ignore the instructor’s limitations.
Review of that flight’s planning and current conditions.
An additional aircraft category rating.
feedback: A signature does not exempt the flight from weather planning.
Limitations remain part of the student’s authorization.
The planning review evaluates the actual route, conditions, and preparation for that flight.
An endorsement of planning does not issue a category rating.
quiz.hint: General proficiency and today’s plan answer different questions.

quiz.question: Which is the best starting point for an added-category or added-class endorsement plan?
options: Assume every add-on has the same requirements.
Use sample numbers from any old endorsement sheet.
Sign the practical-test recommendation before reviewing experience.
Read §61.63 for the requested addition and the applicant’s existing privileges.
feedback: Category and class additions can follow different requirements.
Sample numbering changes and does not define the legal requirement.
The recommendation must follow the eligibility and proficiency review.
The rule and the applicant’s existing privileges determine the required training and testing pathway.
quiz.hint: Identify the exact privilege being added.

quiz.question: A CFI’s recent-experience period ended last month. Which statement is accurate under the ordinary reinstatement rules?
options: The instructor may continue teaching for three more months.
The instructor must stop exercising CFI privileges until reinstated, with the short post-lapse FIRC route potentially available.
The pilot certificate is automatically revoked.
The certificate must always be regained through an initial CFI course.
feedback: The post-lapse FIRC option is not an extension of instructional privileges.
The instructor must first restore privileges through the applicable §61.199 process.
A lapse in CFI recent experience does not automatically revoke the separate pilot certificate.
The rule provides reinstatement pathways rather than universally requiring a new initial course.
quiz.hint: A route to reinstatement does not authorize instruction before reinstatement.

quiz.question: How long must an instructor retain the records prescribed by §61.189?
options: At least three years.
Only until the student earns a certificate.
Exactly 90 days after each endorsement.
Only while employed by the same school.
feedback: The required instructor records have a minimum three-year retention period.
Student certification does not end the instructor’s retention duty.
The solo authorization window and record-retention period serve different purposes.
Changing schools does not erase the individual instructor’s record obligation.
quiz.hint: Distinguish record retention from an authorization’s validity.
